newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China's new tariff unlikely to affect fuel imports.
newsitem.headline: China's new tariff unlikely to affect fuel imports.

text.p: China's decision to double import tariffs on fuel oil to 6.0 percent in April is unlikely to affect the country's imports, Chinese and industry sources said on Wednesday.
Beijing said the new import tariff would be imposed from April 1. The current, temporary rate is 3.0 percent.

The tariff was 12 percent for most of 1996, then was slashed to 3.0 percent in November. A customs official said the cut was to meet increased winter fuel oil demand in China at a time when international prices were hitting five-year highs.
"Now the spring has come and we don't need that much fuel oil for heating, so we have to cancel the temporary tariff and impose a regular one," the official said from Beijing.
Fuel oil is used in power generation, industry and shipping.
A jump in fuel oil buying for stocks before the new rate is imposed is unlikely, a Chinese trader said, noting the recent fall in fuel oil swaps.
"Chinese companies could buy fuel oil now in the spot market before April 1, but if you look at the swaps, prices are weak and there may be no need to buy stocks," the trader said.
The tariffs will not change fuel oil import patterns, traders said.

SINOCHEM, China's state trading firm, imports an average 400,000-500,000 tonnes of fuel oil a month. That slid in late 1996 because of high prices, but has rebounded to about 500,000 tonnes since January a company source said.
"The domestic output is dropping but demand is rising. The only way is to import," the SINOCHEM source said. He declined to estimate China's fuel oil imports in 1997.
Such imports would not be affected by the change in tariffs, he added.
China's fuel oil output totalled 23.0121 million tonnes in 1996, a 17.45 percent fall from 1995, according to the State Statistical Bureau data.
In 1996, China imported 8.540 million tonnes of fuel oil, customs figures showed. The 1995 figures were not available.

Industry sources said Beijing's increasing imports to meet domestic demand could benefit South Korean companies, which have been supplying China with an average of 400,000-500,000 tonnes of fuel oil a month since 1996.
"But if Chinese demand soars significantly, South Korean companies won't be able to handle that," said one Korean trader.
"China will be forced to buy from Japan or Singapore, even though prices are higher in Singapore," he added.
Chinese traders, who have been away from the Singapore market since early February, said South Korea's fuel oil quality is better than that in Singapore and prices are more attractive.
Japan has also been supplying China due to geographic convenience, Chinese traders said.
